messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
The current bug report describes a problem where FastDateParser (FDP) treats a single white-space in the pattern as any number of whitespace characters (`\s*+` in regex), whereas SimpleDateFormat parser (SDP) does not treat whitespace specially and matches whitespace exactly. This mismatch causes FDP to incorrectly parse some input strings that SDP would reject.

Looking at the code of FastDateParser.init(), the method converts the pattern string to a regex pattern stored in `parsePattern` by going through the format fields and calling `Strategy.addRegex()` to append regex fragments to match parts of the date.

From the code of FastDateParser.TextStrategy.addRegex(), regexes for text fields are constructed using `escapeRegex()`, which is of particular interest regarding whitespace handling.

The `escapeRegex` method converts occurrences of whitespace characters in the input text (field values) into the regex pattern `\s*+`, effectively replacing any continuous whitespace by a regex that matches zero or more whitespace characters. This means that a single whitespace character in the input pattern expands to a regex that allows any number (including 0) of whitespace characters when matching actual input dates.

Hence, FastDateParser's pattern-to-regex translation treats whitespace in a more lenient/greedy way than SimpleDateFormat (which matches whitespace literally). This explains why FDP accepts more inputs than SDP and fails to match the SDP behavior exactly, causing the test `testLANG_831()` to fail.

In summary, the root cause is that FastDateParser's regex generation replaces literal whitespace by a more permissive regex pattern (`\s*+`), contrary to SimpleDateFormat's literal whitespace matching. This is seen in the escapeRegex() method at line 310 in the code snippet.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
